planting.note: Set divisions or nursery plugs into thin, rocky limestone soil in the dappled to deep shade under oak-juniper canopy; established colonies spread slowly from a semi-woody base and need little care beyond occasional deep watering the first season.

directions: Hairy tubetongue is a low, spreading subshrub-like perennial found tucked into the rocky, leaf-littered floor of oak-juniper woodlands across the Edwards Plateau and South Texas, where it tolerates the dry shade and thin calcareous soil beneath a closed cedar-brake canopy better than most flowering natives. Fuzzy, two-lipped white to pale-lavender tubular flowers appear in flushes from spring through fall, especially after rain, nestled among soft, hairy, gray-green leaves. It is a key larval host plant for the Texas crescent and vesta crescent butterflies, making it a quietly valuable addition to a native woodland-understory planting even though the flowers themselves are modest. Once established in its preferred lean, well-drained limestone soil, it needs no supplemental irrigation and slowly forms a loose colony by rhizomatous spread.

planting.note: Transplant container-grown shrubs into shaded, north-facing limestone slopes beneath an oak-juniper canopy, matching the deep shade and leaf-duff soil of its few known Hill Country canyon sites; water regularly the first year to establish roots in the shallow, rocky ground.

directions: Texas croton is an exceedingly rare evergreen shrub known from only a handful of shaded limestone canyon slopes on the Edwards Plateau, where it grows beneath a closed oak-juniper canopy far denser and darker than the open savanna and grotto sites typical of most Hill Country natives. Its leathery leaves show a distinctive metallic, silvery-bronze scaling on the undersides and new copper-toned growth, giving it year-round textural interest even though its small yellow-green flowers in late winter are inconspicuous. Slow-growing and long-lived, it depends on the deep, moist leaf duff and sheltered microclimate of the cedar brake floor rather than the thin, sun-baked caliche of adjacent savanna. Because of its restricted native range, it is grown primarily as a conservation-minded specimen for native-plant collectors recreating authentic Edwards Plateau woodland-understory conditions.
